label: bidriware/chemistry/patina-steps
title: How the bidri patina may form
description: Two steps a thesis infers for the bidri patina, zinc dissolving and the copper left behind turning to oxides, beside the finding that the patina's compounds are unidentified.

attrs.aria-label: A bidri piece in the solution

u0003.text: In the solution zinc dissolves first, leaving a surface rich in copper.

u0005.text: Ammonium chloride and potassium nitrate in water

u0006.text: The compounds forming the patina have not been identified.

u0009.text: In nitrate solution the copper-rich surface converts to CuO and Cu2O, which a thesis infers give the black.

u0010.text: X-ray diffraction found simonkolleite, zincite and cuprite, which are white or reddish.

u0012.text: Zinc dissolves first and the copper left behind darkens.

C121.text: La Niece and Martin reported that the compounds forming the black patina had not been identified, and a V&A record calls the exact chemical process still unidentified.

quotes.quote: The compound or compounds forming the patina have not been identified.
The exact chemical process which takes place is still unidentified.

C124.text: An IIT Madras thesis inferred that the copper-enriched surface converts in nitrate solution to CuO and Cu2O, and that these oxides give the black appearance.

quotes.quote: From the current investigation, the following can be inferred
In such a solution zinc dissolves preferentially leading to copper enriched surface, which in nitrate containing solution converts to CuO and Cu2O. These oxides render the black appearance.

C125.text: X-ray diffraction of bidri patinas found simonkolleite, zincite and cuprite as the main crystalline phases, which are white or reddish rather than black.

quotes.quote: identified the three main crystalline components of all the object and experimental patinas analysed:- Simonkolleite, zinc hydroxychloride (Zn5(OH)8 Cl2) Zincite, zinc oxide (ZnO) Cuprite, copper I oxide (Cu2O)
The two zinc compounds identified are white in colour and cuprite appears reddish, so these results do not directly explain the black colouration of the patina.

C131.text: An IIT Madras thesis found that 20 g of ammonium chloride and 5 g of potassium nitrate in 100 ml of water gave a black patina like that from Bidri sand.

quotes.quote: 5g of potassium nitrate (KNO3), 20g of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) was dissolved in 100 ml of de-ionised water
An alternative to Bidri sand has been identified. A mixture of NH4Cl and KNO3 (20g:5g) in 100mL of de-ionized water renders black patina on the surface similar to one seen with Bidri sand.
